why_this_file_is_json: These pointer strings live in JSON, not in the test source, on purpose. The
pointer scanner's citing corpus is CITING_EXTENSIONS ['.md', '.mjs'] under
CITING_ROOTS ['docs', 'plugin'] — so the guard test itself, a .mjs file under
plugin/, is a citing file. Spelling any of these strings as a literal there
would mint a live pointer finding in this repo, and that finding could not be
baselined away, because the guard forbids exactly these strings from entering
the baseline. Unresolvable by construction. '.json' is not a citing
extension, so the strings are inert here.
why_these_strings_are_forbidden: The baseline ratchet's --accept-new refuses to write while any pointer is
PROVABLY wrong — a drift or a broken anchor. It does NOT refuse for a pointer
that merely lacks an anchor, which is accepted debt. Six of the nine pointers
the sweep below repaired were in exactly that anchorless state, so nothing in
the tooling would stop a future maintainer from re-introducing one and
baselining it away. The ordering discipline that protected them lived only in
a plan document; test/pointer-baseline-guard.test.mjs makes it permanent by
asserting these strings never appear in .pointer-baseline.json.
